title: Global Economics: Final Assessment
description: A final assessment covering the key ideas from all three lessons. Reach the passing score to complete the course.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not reviewed or approved by a human (admin); do not give to students.

Comprehensive audit: q4-q6: currencies defined in every prompt; q5: key was the only hedged choice, all choices now parallel and the explanation names the J-curve; q7: key reworded in the same form as the other options; q8: stem no longer asks for 'a concern discussed in this course' and options made parallel; q10 retagged advanced to intermediate (one-step application of the externality idea). Independent-review follow-up: q3, q7, q10 citations corrected; q5 stem no longer states the mechanism and option a no longer contradicts it (cites Saylor 8.12); q8 distractors hedged but wrong; q3 given a product context distinct from l1-q5. Lead QA: q8 key shortened so it no longer stands out or echoes the lesson. Not reviewed or approved by a human.

passing.note: Proposed: 7 of 10 questions (70%). Not approved by a teacher (admin); completion is not recognized until approved.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In one week, a worker in Country E can make 3 tables or 12 lamps, and a worker in Country F can make 2 tables or 4 lamps. Country F exports tables to Country E. Which terms of trade would benefit both countries?

choices.text: 1 table traded for 1 lamp
1 table traded for 5 lamps
1 table traded for 4.5 lamps
1 table traded for 3 lamps

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a country to have a comparative advantage in producing a good?

choices.text: It gives up less of other goods to make it than other countries do
It can make more of the good per worker than other countries can
It exports more of the good than any other country in the world
It protects its producers of the good with a tariff on imports

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In a small importing country, the world price of a toy is $8. At $8, buyers want 500 and domestic firms supply 200 (thousands of toys). A $2 tariff raises the domestic price to $10, where buyers want 460 and domestic firms supply 260. What is the deadweight loss of the tariff, in thousands of dollars? (Enter a number only.)

Hypothetical example (invented currencies): Country C uses the coro (COR), and Country D uses the dena (DEN). The exchange rate is quoted as 1 DEN = 0.8 COR (coros per dena). A bicycle made in Country C sells for 400 COR. How many denas does a buyer in Country D pay, ignoring shipping and taxes? (Enter a number only.)

Hypothetical example (invented currencies): Country C uses the coro (COR), and Country D uses the dena (DEN). The coro depreciates sharply. Sellers keep their prices in their own currencies. Most of Country C's import and export orders for the next few months were signed before the depreciation. What is the most likely short-run effect on Country C's trade balance measured in coros?

choices.text: It improves right away, because Country C's exports become cheaper for foreign buyers
It stays the same, because the signed orders fix both the quantities and their coro values
It worsens at first, because each import costs more coros while quantities change little
It improves at first and then worsens, because buyers switch to new suppliers

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example (invented currencies): Country C uses the coro (COR), and Country D uses the dena (DEN). The dena appreciates against the coro. Which group in Country D is most likely to benefit?

choices.text: Firms in Country D that export goods to Country C
Travelers from Country D on vacation in Country C
Hotels in Country D that host visitors from Country C
Farmers in Country D who compete with imports from Country C

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Country G assembles phones from imported parts. Each phone is exported for $300, and the imported parts for it cost $260. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Country G adds $300 of value per phone, the full price at which it exports
Country G adds $560 of value per phone, the parts cost plus the export price
Country G adds $0 of value per phone, because the parts it uses are imported
Country G adds $40 of value per phone, the export price minus the parts cost

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Country D bans imports from foreign factories that fail its environmental and safety standards. Which statement about this policy is most accurate?

choices.text: It can cut sales for exporters in poorer countries, and its rules can shield domestic firms
It tends to lower the prices of these goods in Country D, because it increases competition among sellers
It mainly shifts the pollution damage to Country D, because the external cost travels with the goods
It tends to lower costs for producers in poorer countries, because cleaner plants are cheaper to run

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A smartphone has a private production cost of $120. Its mining stage causes an assumed external cost of $6 per phone, and its assembly stage causes an assumed external cost of $4 per phone. What is the social cost of one phone, in dollars? (Enter a number only.)
Why might firms choose less supply chain resilience than would be best for society as a whole?

choices.text: Resilience lowers a firm's costs in normal times, so firms tend to overuse it
Disruptions affect just the firm whose own supplier stops making deliveries
Some losses from a disruption fall on customers and workers outside the firm
Extra inventory costs a firm nothing, so it sees little reason to hold more
